1.pericope_label: Therefore thou shalt love the LORD thy God, and keep his charge, and his statutes, and his judgments, and his commandments, alway. And know ye this day: for I speak not with your children which have not known, and which have not seen the chastisement of the LORD your God, his greatness, his mighty hand, and his stretched out arm, And his miracles, and his acts, which he did in the midst of Egypt unto Pharaoh the king of Egypt, and unto all his land; And what he did unto the army of Egypt, unto their horses, and to their chariots; how he made the water of the Red sea to overflow them as they pursued after you, and how the LORD hath destroyed them unto this day; And what he did unto you in the wilderness, until ye came into this place; And what he did unto Dathan and Abiram, the sons of Eliab, the son of Reuben: how the earth opened her mouth, and swallowed them up, and their households, and their tents, and all the substance that was in their possession, in the midst of all Israel: But your eyes have seen all the great acts of the LORD which he did.

schools.summary: Calvin reads the order of the sentence as the argument: love is asked for before obedience because obedience extracted by fear cannot please God, and Moses deliberately leads by grace rather than by menace. He treats the piling up of names for the Law as a sign that nothing needed for regulating a life has been left out, and glosses the first of them as a fence keeping life from straying either way. On the syntax he weighs joining know ye to the following noun against letting it stand alone, prefers the latter, and objects that the noun is too general to be narrowed to chastisement. Gill supplies the grounds — God’s own greatness and his multiplying of the nation — and reads the wilderness clause as covering the corrections rather than the kindnesses of those years.

Henry works the connection between the two halves of the opening command: love will work in obedience, and only the obedience that flows from love is acceptable. He hears priestly language in keeping the charge and applies it to a whole nation of priests. On the memories he addresses the seniors, those old enough to remember Egypt, and reads each judgment as a mercy to Israel — Egypt ruined to force their release, its army drowned to prevent their re-enslavement, and the Reubenite rebellion crushed because deliverance from insurrection at home is as real a kindness as deliverance from invasion abroad.

Clarke grounds the command in the state of the heart: where the love of God is absent there can be neither obedience nor happiness, the heart being empty of all good and therefore miserable. Wesley keeps close to the words — knowing here means acknowledging and considering with thankfulness — presses the continuing force of destroyed unto this day into Egypt’s lasting weakness and Israel’s consequent safety, and observes that some of the hearers had seen part of these things and some the whole, which is reason enough to make use of them long afterwards.

Ellicott denies any break at the chapter division, so that the command to love follows directly on the promise of a multiplied nation, and renders the charge literally as what is to be kept, with alway as all the days. He dates the audience by simple arithmetic, everyone under twenty at the Exodus still being alive, and finds emphasis in the placing of the adjectives describing the hand and arm of God. He also uses the mention of Dathan and Abiram against the claim that Deuteronomy knows no priesthood beyond the tribe. Keil takes the clause about the children as a verbless parenthesis needing a supplied predicate, and distinguishes the desert-born from those who had watched the plagues as boys.

debates: Whether know ye governs the following noun or stands on its own.
Whether that noun means chastisement or something more general.
Which generation Moses is addressing, and how old they now are.
What keeping the charge covers.
outliers: Ellicott argues from this verse that the author of Deuteronomy cannot have been ignorant of a priesthood narrower than the tribe of Levi, since the point of the rebellion it recalls was precisely that distinction.
Henry reads the destruction of Egypt as ransom money paid for Israel, so that a famous kingdom was spent rather than a people left unredeemed.
Wesley and Calvin agree independently that destroyed unto this day describes a still-running effect rather than a past event.
Gill takes the wilderness clause as pointing to the corrections of those years rather than the provisions.
themes: Therefore thou shalt love the LORD thy God
Keep his charge alway
Not with your children, but with you
What he did in the midst of Egypt
Dathan and Abiram swallowed up
Your eyes have seen

8.pericope_label: Therefore shall ye keep all the commandments which I command you this day, that ye may be strong, and go in and possess the land, whither ye go to possess it; And that ye may prolong your days in the land, which the LORD sware unto your fathers to give unto them and to their seed, a land that floweth with milk and honey. For the land, whither thou goest in to possess it, is not as the land of Egypt, from whence ye came out, where thou sowedst thy seed, and wateredst it with thy foot, as a garden of herbs: But the land, whither ye go to possess it, is a land of hills and valleys, and drinketh water of the rain of heaven: A land which the LORD thy God careth for: the eyes of the LORD thy God are always upon it, from the beginning of the year even unto the end of the year.

schools.summary: Gill separates entering the land from continuing in it, and hangs only the second on obedience. On the comparison he is topographical before he is devotional: hills and valleys cannot be irrigated the way a flat country can, which is why Canaan must drink rain, and the arrangement is healthier as well as easier, since the vapours of the flooded Nile were unwholesome and its season shut people indoors. He grants God a general providence over all the earth and claims a particular one here, on the ground that this was the place chosen for his residence and his worship.

Henry treats the whole passage as two promises, possession and continuance, both hanging on the same condition, and notices what Moses does not do: he gives no military instruction, because a people true to their religion have their strength in that. He makes the Egyptian labour vivid against Israel’s ease, and reads the rain as a standing lesson in dependence, the more cheerful the obedience the closer the reliance. He also faces the land’s later barrenness and takes it as evidence for his reading rather than against it: the fruitfulness was the blessing’s, not the soil’s.

Clarke argues from the judgments just recalled to the duty now enjoined, and explains watering with the foot from the practice of Egyptian irrigation, including the trench banked up by the foot and a treadle-worked lifting machine. Wesley widens the labour to everything the feet had to do in Egypt, points out that the inundation often failed and that its mud hardened and needed watering again, and lists four advantages of rain over flood — ease, pleasantness, healthfulness, and certainty. He makes the conditional promise a kindness rather than a threat, since it binds a people by their own interest to what their happiness depends on.

Ellicott observes that the commandment is singular, one course of action rather than a list, and that possessing means finishing the conquest in detail. He renders the last clause as a land the LORD seeks, gathers the parallels where God espies or searches out a resting place for his people, hears the better country behind it, and honestly records the Jewish objection that God sends rain on lands where nobody lives. Keil keeps to the plain sense: God inquires after this land and his eyes rest on it the year round, and its dependence on him is precisely what suits it to a people meant to live wholly to their God.

debates: What watering with the foot describes: carrying water, banking channels with the foot, or working a lifting machine by foot.
Whether the land’s later barrenness tells against the description here.
Whether God’s seeking out this land can mean anything peculiar, given that he waters lands where no man lives.
Whether the commandment here is one thing or many.
outliers: Ellicott reads the clause typologically, as pointing past Canaan to the country prepared for God’s people.
Henry suggests the rain is called the river of God in deliberate contempt of the Nile.
Wesley argues that making the promise conditional was itself a mercy, since it tied the people’s interest to their obedience.
Gill prefers the health of Canaan to its fertility as the point of the contrast, noting that the Nile’s flood confined the Egyptians indoors for weeks together.
Clarke supports his reading of the phrase from irrigation machinery still in use in his own day.
themes: Keep the commandment, and go in and possess
Not as the land of Egypt
Watered with thy foot
A land of hills and valleys
Drinketh water of the rain of heaven
The eyes of the LORD always upon it

13.pericope_label: And it shall come to pass, if ye shall hearken diligently unto my commandments which I command you this day, to love the LORD your God, and to serve him with all your heart and with all your soul, That I will give you the rain of your land in his due season, the first rain and the latter rain, that thou mayest gather in thy corn, and thy wine, and thine oil. And I will send grass in thy fields for thy cattle, that thou mayest eat and be full. Take heed to yourselves, that your heart be not deceived, and ye turn aside, and serve other gods, and worship them; And then the LORD's wrath be kindled against you, and he shut up the heaven, that there be no rain, and that the land yield not her fruit; and lest ye perish quickly from off the good land which the LORD giveth you.

schools.summary: Gill locates the temptation inside the promise: a people taught to watch the sky for their harvest are the likeliest to end up worshipping it, and the pull of ancestral custom, antiquity, and sheer numbers does the rest. He also explains why idolatry provokes God beyond other sins, as an offence against his being and not only his law. Calvin reads the repeated take heed as an indirect indictment of human nature, which will fall into the snare of superstition the moment it stops guarding itself, and refuses to treat turning aside as a venial excess: a corrupted worship is apostasy, however light men hold it and however sincerely they plead their intentions.

Henry balances the two halves of the sanction. In due season means rain neither withheld when the ground wants it nor sent in excess, and the promise stands for every seasonable mercy rather than for weather alone. On the warning he presses the avoidable character of the fall — a little care would have prevented it, which is what will make the ruin bitter — and lays the consequences out in order: anger provoked, good things withdrawn, evil brought on. His closing turn is that a good land aggravates rather than softens the loss, since its goodness gives no security once its people are ripe for ruin.

Clarke supplies the agricultural fact the promise depends on: the November rain that lets the seed grow and the April rain that fills the ear, with almost nothing between, so that either failing destroys the harvest. From the conditional form of the promise he argues that rain is not left to a general providence but governed by a particular one. Wesley illustrates the threat from the storehouse of rain whose doors God opens and shuts, and turns the blessing into a caution of his own: godliness carries the promise of this life, but God’s favour gives more gladness than any increase of corn or wine or oil.

Ellicott identifies the passage as the formal sanction of the charge, a pattern he traces across the codes and into the New Testament, and dates the two rains to the ninth and first months. He preserves two Jewish readings without insisting on them — that serving with the whole heart points to prayer, which was all that remained to Israel in exile, and that gathering in is itself a promise, thou and not thine enemies — and notes the further blessing in being full, since a man may eat and go unsatisfied. He also fixes the moment of danger as the moment of satisfaction. Keil reads the section as the structural close of the discourse, blessing and curse together.

debates: Whether serving with all the heart means prayer in particular.
Whether rain is governed by general providence or by a particular one.
What it is that deceives the heart: the visible influence of the heavens, the custom of the nations, or our own proneness to superstition.
Whether a corrupted worship is a lesser fault than open apostasy.
outliers: Gill argues that the very blessing promised here is what makes star-worship a live temptation.
Ellicott keeps a Jewish gloss that gathering in implies thou, and not thine enemies.
Ellicott notes that being full is a distinct blessing from being fed, since it is possible to eat and not be satisfied.
Wesley sets the favour of God above the increase of corn and wine and oil, even while granting that godliness carries the promise of this life.
Henry holds that the goodness of the land will aggravate the judgment rather than avert it.
themes: If ye shall hearken diligently
The first rain and the latter rain
Grass in thy fields for thy cattle
Take heed that your heart be not deceived
He shut up the heaven
Ye perish quickly from off the good land

18.pericope_label: Therefore shall ye lay up these my words in your heart and in your soul, and bind them for a sign upon your hand, that they may be as frontlets between your eyes.

schools.summary: Calvin distinguishes the two nouns — with soul beside it, heart carries the mind, so the Law must be both understood and loved — and reads laying up as hiding deeply rather than merely remembering. On the sign and the frontlets he is emphatic that God cared nothing for the bands themselves: they were set where ornaments are set, to keep meeting the wearer and rousing him, and that purpose is what condemns both the hunt for a reputation of holiness through finery and the notion that an outward dress discharges a duty. He ends on succession, the Law kept in vigour because each generation teaches the next. Gill breaks the command into treasuring, retaining and loving, and names its use: an antidote against apostasy and idolatry.

Henry gathers the verse into three rules — the heart filled with the word as a store-house, the eyes fixed on it as on something bound to the hand and set between the eyes, the tongue employed about it, above all with children. He grounds the first on the order of things, since no good practice appears in the conversation without good principles within, and turns the second from dress into conduct, God’s judgments laid before us as the guide of our way and the rule of our work. On the third he is most insistent: children are to be taught the service of God as more needful than manners or a trade, and nothing does more for the continuance of religion in a nation than their education.

Wesley reproduces Henry’s three rules almost word for word, including the store-house image, the hand always in view and the frontlets that cannot be avoided, and the priority of teaching children the word above the rules of decency or the calling they are to live by. Clarke adds nothing but a cross-reference to the earlier passage where the same charge stands, which is itself worth registering: this section of the discourse is deliberate repetition, not new legislation.

Ellicott points out that the connective is a plain and rather than an inference, so the verse can be read as continuing the threat immediately before it — you will perish from the land, and you will take these words to heart — and he passes on the Jewish comment that Israel would remember them in captivity if not sooner. He then rejects that as the primary sense, since the promise of multiplied days that follows points the other way, and classes it as an application drawn from what actually happened. He also notes that the injunctions are a repetition of an earlier passage.

debates: Whether the opening word is an inference from the threat before it or a simple connective.
Whether binding the words on hand and forehead is a literal practice or a figure for keeping them in view.
What is added by naming the soul alongside the heart.
Whether this section legislates anything new or repeats an earlier charge.
outliers: Ellicott preserves a reading he does not accept, that Israel would take the words to heart in exile if not before, and explains why he thinks it an application rather than the sense.
Calvin argues that the very purpose of the outward sign refutes the use later made of it as a badge of piety.
Wesley’s note here follows Henry’s three rules so closely as to be an abridgement of them rather than an independent judgment.
Henry rates the religious education of children above both manners and trade, and makes it the security of a nation’s religion.
Clarke offers only a cross-reference, treating the passage as a repetition of ground already covered.
themes: Lay up these words in your heart
And in your soul
Bind them for a sign upon your hand
Frontlets between your eyes
Teaching them to the children

21.pericope_label: That your days may be multiplied, and the days of your children, in the land which the LORD sware unto your fathers to give them, as the days of heaven upon the earth. For if ye shall diligently keep all these commandments which I command you, to do them, to love the LORD your God, to walk in all his ways, and to cleave unto him; Then will the LORD drive out all these nations from before you, and ye shall possess greater nations and mightier than yourselves. Every place whereon the soles of your feet shall tread shall be yours: from the wilderness and Lebanon, from the river, the river Euphrates, even unto the uttermost sea shall your coast be. There shall no man be able to stand before you: for the LORD your God shall lay the fear of you and the dread of you upon all the land that ye shall tread upon, as he hath said unto you.

schools.summary: Gill works throughout to keep the promises inside their stated limits. Obedience means practice and not notional knowledge; the nations are dispossessed gradually rather than at a stroke; the clause about the sole of the foot is bounded by the borders named immediately after it, so it cannot be stretched into a title to any ground an Israelite happens to stand on. On the last verse he reasons from scale: no man able to stand cannot mean an individual champion, since no army of six hundred thousand would have feared one, so it must mean no nation however much greater and mightier.

Wesley reads the days of heaven as the measure of the tenure, and maps the four borders — the wilderness of Sin, Lebanon, Euphrates, the midland sea — while separating outright possession from mere dominion and hanging both on obedience; he concludes that Israel’s sins cut them short of the grant and that Solomon alone reached its edge. Clarke arrives at the same verdict from the fulfilment rather than the terms, observing that despite all the provocations between, the reign of Solomon did extend from the Euphrates to the border of Egypt.

Ellicott is the only witness here who reads outward rather than inward. He notices that the oath was to give the land to the fathers themselves, records without ridicule the Jewish inference that the resurrection is therefore taught in the Law, and points to the difficulty as the New Testament states it, that Abraham received not a foot of ground and was promised all of it. He lets a Jewish commentator define walking in God’s ways as imitating his compassion and cleaving to him as cleaving to the wise, and renders both into New Testament language. On the closing verse he takes fear and dread as falling on the near and the far respectively, and lets the promise run as wide as the words allow.

debates: Whether the promise of every place the foot treads is limited to Canaan or unlimited.
Whether the grant was ever fulfilled, and when.
Whether the oath being made to the fathers rather than to their descendants implies a resurrection.
Whether no man able to stand means no individual or no nation.
outliers: Ellicott declines to dismiss a Jewish resurrection argument as fanciful, on the ground that the belief behind it is a fact whatever one makes of the reasoning.
Ellicott renders a rabbinic gloss on cleaving to God into New Testament terms without qualification.
Gill and Wesley independently reject the wider application of the promise about the sole of the foot.
Wesley holds that Israel’s sins cut them short of a grant that was theirs by right of promise.
Ellicott lets the promise of dread run as far as the words permit, in the same breath in which the others narrow the promise of land.
themes: That your days may be multiplied
As the days of heaven upon the earth
To walk in all his ways and to cleave unto him
Every place whereon the soles of your feet shall tread
The fear of you and the dread of you

26.pericope_label: Behold, I set before you this day a blessing and a curse; A blessing, if ye obey the commandments of the LORD your God, which I command you this day: And a curse, if ye will not obey the commandments of the LORD your God, but turn aside out of the way which I command you this day, to go after other gods, which ye have not known.

schools.summary: Calvin reads the pair as the seal on everything already taught, hope and fear together, and stresses that Moses is announcing consequences rather than merely stating duties. He also draws attention to the double claim in the verse — God is the Law’s author, and Moses is the one who commands after him — and explains the second as a check on the pride that would rather hear God directly than through the servant he speaks by. Gill spells the two outcomes into particulars of body, estate, family and flock, indoors and out, and refuses to confine the curse to this life; he also notes that the appeal is made to every individual, the matter concerning them all.

Henry treats the verse as the peroration of the discourse and analyses how it works: the blessing and the curse are the promises and threatenings gathered into two words, and they take hold of hope and fear, the two handles by which a soul is managed. He identifies three things Moses does with them — explains them so their weight is felt, confirms them from his commission so that neither is dismissed as fantasy, and puts the choice to the people — and observes that this is remarkably fair dealing from a man who had been publicly accused of blinding those he led.

Clarke makes the verse the ground of an argument for free will: precepts backed by promise and threat presuppose a power to obey or refuse, since an agent that is not free can be neither punished nor rewarded, as a falling stone is neither. He holds that Scripture declares a self-determining will throughout, that nothing short of omnipotence could override it, and that God never does — leaving the terms as obedience with divine help and life, or refusal of that help and death. Wesley works on a smaller point, that the gods in question are ones Israel has no acquaintance with and no experience of, unlike the God they are being asked to leave.
Ellicott notes that one of the Jewish divisions of Deuteronomy begins at this word, and renders the two nouns without articles, as blessing and cursing distributed by the condition attached to each.

debates: Whether setting a blessing and a curse before men presupposes a free and self-determining will.
Whether the curse reaches beyond this life.
Why Moses asserts his own commission alongside God’s authorship of the Law.
Whether the blessing and the curse are two dispensations or one law under two aspects.
outliers: Clarke argues from the form of the command to the freedom of the will, and illustrates it from a stone that can be neither rewarded nor blamed for obeying gravity.
Henry and Calvin independently describe the blessing and the curse as working on hope and fear.
Calvin reads Moses’ insistence on his own ministry as a rebuke to those who would rather hear God without a mediator.
Henry points out the fairness of putting the choice openly to men who had once accused Moses of blinding them.
Wesley notes that the attraction of the other gods rests on no experience of them at all.
themes: Behold, I set before you this day
A blessing, if ye obey
A curse, if ye will not obey
Turning aside out of the way
Gods which ye have not known

29.pericope_label: And it shall come to pass, when the LORD thy God hath brought thee in unto the land whither thou goest to possess it, that thou shalt put the blessing upon mount Gerizim, and the curse upon mount Ebal. Are they not on the other side Jordan, by the way where the sun goeth down, in the land of the Canaanites, which dwell in the champaign over against Gilgal, beside the plains of Moreh? For ye shall pass over Jordan to go in to possess the land which the LORD your God giveth you, and ye shall possess it, and dwell therein. And ye shall observe to do all the statutes and judgments which I set before you this day.

schools.summary: Calvin explains the design of making the people pronounce the words themselves: a declaration by the Levites alone would have bound them less than their own spoken assent, which acts as a formal ratification, and the ceremony is deferred until they are in the land because the sight of it confirms the covenant. He notes that the two mountains face each other so the divided tribes could answer one another, and treats the closing question as a vehement affirmation designed to steady people whose unbelief had survived every previous deliverance. Gill fixes the location against a rabbinic tradition by the plain fact of distance, and grounds Israel’s title in the gift alone.

Henry records the appointment of the ceremony and then turns it forward. The blessing and curse published on the two hills become, in his hands, the position of anyone who has broken a law and has no remedy in himself, and he reads the gospel as setting the same alternative before men a second time.

Clarke derives both names etymologically — Gerizim from cutting or reaping, and so from fertility; Ebal from roughness or from white stones, and so from barrenness — and turns the pair into a standing parable of the land’s dependence on its people’s obedience, its fruitfulness always a blessing earned and its bareness always a judgment incurred. He extends the claim to the whole country, arguing that a naturally stony land could never have carried its ancient population without a particular providence. Wesley works on the verb, which means to pronounce rather than to place, and on the site, recalling that Moreh was among Abram’s first stopping places, so that the tribes heard the covenant read where the promise had first been given.

Ellicott collects the Targum renderings and the practice of turning toward each mountain in turn, and uses them to date the traditional understanding. His strongest observation is topographical: the phrase about the setting sun fixes the speaker east of Jordan opposite Jericho, and travellers on that spot have seen the sun go down precisely in the gap between Ebal and Gerizim. He corrects plains to oaks or terebinths, ties the site to the first promise made to Abram, and marks the structural seam here between the exposition of Israel’s relation to God and the laws of the land that follow, noting that the analysis matters because the authorship of those chapters is disputed.

debates: What putting the blessing and the curse on the mountains means in practice.
Whether the names Gerizim and Ebal were given for the fertility and barrenness of the two hills.
How far the mountains lay from the Jordan crossing.
Whether the closing question is a real question or an emphatic assertion.
Where this section of the book ends and the next begins.
outliers: Ellicott treats the direction of the setting sun as evidence for the speaker’s standpoint east of Jordan.
Clarke argues that the natural poverty of the soil makes the ancient population of the land an argument for particular providence.
Gill corrects a rabbinic tradition about the mountains by the distance from Jericho.
Wesley and Ellicott independently connect the site with the first promise given to Abram at Moreh.
Calvin holds that the people’s own voices, not the Levites’, are what make the ceremony binding.
themes: The blessing upon Gerizim, the curse upon Ebal
By the way where the sun goeth down
Beside the plains of Moreh
Ye shall pass over Jordan
Observe to do all the statutes
